title: Tier III Checkpoint II — An EAP/ESP Course

points.h: Ground the Course in Deep Needs Analysis
pts: Conduct genuine target-situation analysis for the specific learner group this course serves, following Unit 65's ESP framework.
Identify the specific genres — academic or professional — the course must build toward, rather than defaulting to generic content.
Involve subject specialists or workplace stakeholders in this analysis wherever feasible.

v: Interview questions; sample documents from the target situation

items: Interview two or three stakeholders: a nursing lecturer, a ward sister, a recent graduate.
Ask what English tasks nurses do in their studies and at work, how often, and which cause problems.
Collect real (anonymized) samples: a care plan, a handover sheet, a lecture outline.
Give learners a short present-situation questionnaire and a diagnostic writing task.
Draw up a map of the six to eight genres the course must build towards, in order of priority.
For an engineering course, interview a site engineer and a faculty member; collect a site report and a lab report.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A genre priority map for the nursing course (written for this book):

lines: 1. Nursing care plan (written, weekly in clinical postings).
2. Verbal handover between shifts (spoken, daily).
3. Lecture on anatomy or pharmacology (listening, several times a week).
4. Explaining procedures to patients, often in another language (mediation, daily).
5. Reflective clinical journal (written, assessed by the college).
A: What English causes most trouble in the ward?
B: The handover. Students write notes well enough, but freeze when speaking to the next shift.

blocks.x: Stakeholder interviews shift priorities in ways a teacher alone might not predict (Dudley-Evans and St John 1998).

body: Purpose: to show the course aimed at real target genres. Content: a compass with ‘care plan’, ‘handover’, ‘lecture’ and ‘explaining to patients’ at the four points, and a nursing student at the centre holding a map. Style: clean, professional. Board version: a cross with four labels.

items: Google Forms (free) for the learner questionnaire.
A phone voice recorder (free) for stakeholder interviews, with consent.

blocks.x: Printed interview sheets and a paper questionnaire.

points.h: Build Academic or Professional Writing In
pts: Design at least one substantial writing strand addressing this course's relevant genre — an academic essay, a professional report.
Apply Unit 54's genre-teaching cycle to this strand explicitly, moving from deconstruction to independent construction.
Include explicit hedging and argumentation-structure teaching appropriate to the target genre's conventions.

v: Four weeks, two sessions a week
Two anonymized model care plans; a stage checklist

items: Build the context: learners discuss a patient case in groups, in any language.
Deconstruct a model care plan: identify stages (assessment, diagnosis, goals, interventions, evaluation) and language features (Unit 54).
Joint construction: the class writes a care plan together for a new case, with the teacher scribing.
Independent construction: learners write a care plan for a third case.
Add a reflective journal entry later in the strand, with explicit teaching of hedging and argument (Unit 61).
For an EAP course, the strand could build towards a short research report or an argumentative essay.
Support: sentence frames for each stage.

blocks.x: Language features from the model (written for this book):

lines: Goal: Patient will be able to walk to the bathroom unassisted within 48 hours.
Intervention: Assist patient to sit up every four hours.
Evaluation: Goal partially met; patient walked with one person assisting.
This may have been because I did not explain the procedure clearly enough.
It seems likely that the patient was anxious rather than uncooperative.

blocks.x: Care plans favour ‘will’ and imperatives; reflective writing needs hedging and cause–effect reasoning.

body: Purpose: to show the genre cycle applied to a professional genre. Content: four steps up a staircase: ‘context’ (group round a patient bed), ‘model’ (an annotated care plan), ‘together’ (teacher at board with class), ‘alone’ (a student writing). Style: professional, warm. Board version: four steps with labels.

items: Google Docs (free) for shared joint construction.

blocks.x: Joint construction on the board, copied by learners into notebooks.

points.h: Include a Listening and Note-Taking Strand
pts: Where the target context involves lectures, briefings, or extended monologic input, build in explicit note-taking skill development.
Use real or realistic recordings from the target domain, rather than generic listening materials, wherever possible.
Teach discourse markers and structure-recognition specific to this domain's typical spoken genres.

v: Short recordings of subject lectures (with permission); a note-taking template

items: Record three short extracts from real nursing lectures (with the lecturers’ permission).
Teach discourse markers that signal structure: ‘There are three main types…’, ‘The key point here is…’, ‘By contrast…’ (Unit 62).
Learners listen once for structure and draw a skeleton outline.
They listen again and complete a structured template.
Pairs compare notes and use them to answer a clinical question.
For handover, learners listen to a recorded role-played handover and complete a handover sheet.
Support: provide a partly completed outline.
Challenge: learners take notes without a template and then compare with a model.

blocks.x: A lecture extract and notes (written for this book):

lines: Lecturer: ‘Now, there are three main routes of drug administration we’ll cover today. First, oral… Second, parenteral, which includes intravenous and intramuscular… And third, topical. The key point with parenteral routes is speed of absorption.’
Notes: Drug routes (3): 1. oral 2. parenteral (IV, IM): fast absorption 3. topical.

blocks.x: Recordings from the learners’ own college are more relevant than generic listening materials.

body: Purpose: to show the move from structure to detail. Content: a lecture slide with three bullet points on the left; on the right, a learner’s notebook showing first a skeleton, then filled notes with arrows and abbreviations. Style: realistic. Board version: an outline with three numbers.

items: Audacity (free, open source) for trimming recordings.

blocks.x: The teacher reads a lecture script aloud at natural speed.

points.h: Consider Literary or Rich Authentic Texts
pts: Where appropriate to the course's aims, include at least one genuinely rich authentic text for deeper stylistic or cultural engagement.
This need not be literary fiction specifically — a rich, well-crafted piece of professional or academic writing can serve a similar function.
Use this text for genuine response and analysis, not just comprehension-check questions.

v: One rich, well-crafted text about nursing

items: Choose one rich text: a short memoir extract, a well-written essay by a nurse, or a poem about care (checking copyright).
Learners read for personal response first: What did you feel? What did you recognize?
Discuss stylistic choices: word choice, point of view, what is left unsaid (Unit 63).
Connect to professional values: compassion, dignity, communication.
Learners write a short personal response in their reflective journal.
Use a text from an Indian writer in translation, and discuss what the translator had to decide.
Support: pre-teach six key words and give a short summary in the home language.

lines: Which sentence would you remember on a difficult night shift? Why?
The writer never names the patient’s illness. Why might that be?
S1: The writer only says ‘she held my hand longer than usual’. It shows she was afraid, without saying it.

blocks.x: A rich text gives learners something to think and feel about, not only to comprehend.

body: Purpose: to suggest deeper engagement with a rich text. Content: an open book on a nurse’s station at night, with a single highlighted line glowing softly. Style: quiet, reflective. Board version: an open book with one line underlined.

items: Project Gutenberg (free) for public-domain texts, such as extracts from Florence Nightingale’s Notes on Nursing (1859).

blocks.x: A photocopied short text or a passage copied on the board.

pts: Where the target context involves cross-linguistic communication, design explicit mediation practice — summarising, explaining across languages.
Draw on learners' full linguistic repertoire deliberately here, rather than defaulting to English-only classroom practice throughout.
Assess mediation using the CEFR's mediation scales as a starting reference point.

v: An English discharge summary (written for this book); role cards

items: In pairs, one learner is the nurse, the other is a patient or family member who speaks mainly Kannada, Telugu, Urdu or Hindi.
The nurse reads a short English discharge summary.
The nurse explains the key instructions to the patient in the patient’s language, simplifying and checking understanding.
Swap roles with a new summary.
The reverse: a patient explains symptoms in the home language, and the nurse writes an English note for the doctor.
Support: highlight the key instructions in the summary before the task.
Challenge: add a family member who asks difficult questions.

blocks.x: An extract from a discharge summary (written for this book):

lines: Take one tablet twice daily after meals for five days. Avoid lifting heavy objects for two weeks. Return if you notice fever or swelling at the wound site.

blocks.x: Assessment focus, based on CEFR mediation descriptors (Council of Europe 2020): Can the nurse identify the key points? Explain them clearly for this listener? Check understanding?

lines: A: What did you find hardest?
B: ‘Wound site’. I had to show the place with my hand as well as say it in Kannada.

body: Purpose: to show mediation as a professional skill. Content: a nurse sitting beside an elderly patient and a family member, holding an English document; speech bubbles in Kannada script flow towards the patient, and a checkmark bubble returns. Style: warm, respectful, Indian hospital setting. Board version: a document, an arrow, a person.

items: None required; mediation is best practised face to face.

blocks.x: Printed discharge summaries and role cards.

body: The CEFR Companion Volume (Council of Europe 2020) includes scales for mediating a text, mediating concepts and mediating communication, and it explicitly allows for mediation between different languages. It is one of the few international frameworks that describes this everyday multilingual skill.

pts: If the course leads toward a specific exam, apply Unit 66's ethical, balanced exam-preparation principles rather than narrow drilling alone.
Otherwise, design task-specific rubrics reflecting the course's own real-world performance standards, per Unit 46.
Communicate realistic expectations to learners and any relevant institutional stakeholders from the outset.

v: The genre map; any exam requirements

items: List every assessment decision the course requires: college marks, progress checks, and any external exam.
For course assessment, write task-specific rubrics for the care plan and the handover (Unit 46).
If some learners plan to take an external exam, such as the Occupational English Test or IELTS, plan a short, clearly separated preparation module using Unit 66’s principles.
Write a one-page statement for learners and the college on what the course can and cannot promise.
Involve learners in co-constructing one rubric (Unit 46).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A statement of expectations (written for this book):

lines: This course will help you write care plans, give handovers and follow lectures in English more confidently. It is not an exam-coaching course. For those planning to take an external English test, we offer four optional sessions on format and strategy near the end. We cannot guarantee any exam score, which depends on many factors, including your practice outside class.

blocks.x: Honesty at the start keeps the course focused on the target situation.

body: Purpose: to show course assessment and exam preparation as distinct. Content: a main road labelled ‘course: care plans, handovers, lectures’, with a short, clearly marked side road labelled ‘optional exam module’ that rejoins it. Style: clean map. Board version: a line with a small loop.

items: Google Docs (free) for rubrics and the expectations statement.

blocks.x: Printed rubrics given to learners in week 1.

pts: Identify one open question about this course worth investigating through a genuine action-research cycle across its first run.
Plan concrete evidence collection — student work samples, brief surveys — built into the course's regular rhythm, not added as an afterthought.
Use findings to refine the course's next iteration, continuing the cycle beyond this first checkpoint.

v: The course plan; simple evidence instruments

items: Identify one open question about the course (Unit 67).
Plan the evidence to collect within normal teaching: work samples, short surveys, observation notes.
Collect a baseline in week 1.
Collect the same evidence at weeks 6 and 12.
Use the findings to revise the course before its second run.
Invite a colleague to observe two handover practice sessions with a focused task (Unit 68).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A course research question (written for this book):

lines: Does allowing learners to plan handovers in their home language before speaking in English increase the completeness of their English handovers?
Evidence: a checklist of eight handover items scored from recordings; a two-question learner survey; teacher notes.
Built-in timing: recordings already made in weeks 4, 8 and 12 for course assessment.

blocks.x: Evidence built into the course rhythm is far easier to collect than evidence added afterwards.

body: Purpose: to show evidence collection woven into teaching. Content: a twelve-week course timeline with small magnifying-glass icons at weeks 1, 6 and 12. Style: clean infographic. Board version: a line with three marks.

items: Google Sheets (free) for recording checklist scores.

blocks.x: A paper checklist for each recording.

body: Choose a research question you genuinely do not know the answer to. If you are sure what the result will be, it is a demonstration, not an investigation.

pts: Identify at least one unit where existing materials genuinely don't fit, and apply this tier's materials-writing craft to develop original content.
Pilot this material with real learners and revise based on what actually happens in the room.
This closes Tier III's second checkpoint the same way the first did: proof that specialist depth combines into one coherent, teachable whole.

v: Two sessions; plus teacher writing time
Design sheet; model handover recording or script; A/B patient cards

items: Identify the gap: no available material teaches spoken handover for Indian ward contexts.
Complete an aim-first design sheet (Unit 69).
Write a model handover script, patient cards with an information gap, and a checklist.
Pilot with one group; note difficulties on both grading dials (language and task).
Revise and file version 2 with a revision log.
Adapt the same structure for a bank teller’s shift report or a site engineer’s daily briefing.
Support: a handover frame (identify, situation, background, assessment, recommendation).
Challenge: learners handle an unexpected question from the incoming nurse.

blocks.x: A model handover (written for this book):

lines: A: This is Mrs Fatima Begum, bed 12, 64 years old. She’s day two after a hip replacement.
A: Her pain is controlled with the prescribed medication. She walked to the chair this morning with assistance.
A: Her blood pressure was a bit high at 6 a.m., 150 over 90. Please check it again at ten.

blocks.x: Pilot note: learners could read the card but paused before numbers. Language dial: add practice saying blood pressure and times aloud. Task dial: fine. This closes the checkpoint as Unit 60 closed the first: specialist depth combined into one coherent, teachable course.

body: Figure 70.8 The whole course on a page

Purpose: to show all strands combined. Content: a twelve-week grid with coloured strands (writing, listening, rich text, mediation, assessment, research, materials) running across the weeks, labelled with Units 61–69. Style: clear course-map infographic. Board version: a table with seven rows.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a colour-coded course map.

blocks.x: A course map drawn on chart paper.

body: Choose one group of learners with a clear target situation. Interview one stakeholder, list three target genres, and sketch a four-week course map with one strand for each genre. Then write one original material for the strand where you have nothing suitable.

dek: Unit 70 of 100: closing this stretch of Tier III by designing a full EAP or ESP course end-to-end, drawing Units 61 through 69 together in one piece of real planning.

aims.x: This checkpoint unit brings Units 61–69 together in one piece of real planning: a complete English for Specific Purposes course. The worked example throughout is a twelve-week course, English for Nursing Studies, for first-year B.Sc. Nursing students at a college in Karnataka (a scenario written for this book). The learners are mostly B1, study in English, care for patients who mostly speak Kannada, Telugu, Urdu or Hindi, and some hope to work abroad. The same steps apply to any EAP or ESP course.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: ground a course in target-situation and present-situation analysis with stakeholder input;
build a writing strand around a genre the target situation actually demands;
design a listening and note-taking strand from domain-specific input;
include one rich authentic text and use it for real response;
plan mediation tasks that draw on learners’ full linguistic repertoire;
design assessment that is realistic, ethical and aligned with the course’s aims;
build one action research question into the first run of a course;
identify where original materials are needed, write them and pilot them.

why: Why this matters. Checkpoint I proved a single advanced unit could combine this tier's early depth. This checkpoint proves the same at full course scale, before the tier's final stretch.

background.x: Course design in ESP has a long tradition. Tom Hutchinson and Alan Waters (1987) argued that ESP is an approach, not a product: all decisions about content and method follow from the learner’s reason for learning. Tony Dudley-Evans and Maggie Jo St John (1998) developed the distinction between target-situation analysis (what learners will need to do) and present-situation analysis (what they can do now), and emphasized collaboration with subject specialists. Helen Basturkmen (2010) showed through case studies how ESP courses are developed in practice, and Kathleen Graves (2000) offers a general framework for designing language courses that moves from needs through goals, content, materials and assessment to evaluation.

Genre research gives ESP course designers their content. John Swales (1990) defined genres through the communicative purposes shared by a discourse community, and Ken Hyland (2006) showed how EAP teaching can make these purposes and conventions visible to learners. Unit 54 introduced the genre-teaching cycle; Unit 61 applied it to academic writing; Unit 62 to lectures and note-taking; Unit 63 to literature and rich texts; Unit 64 to translation and mediation; and Unit 65 to ESP course design.

The CEFR Companion Volume added descriptors for mediation, which describe how users relay, explain and summarize meaning across languages and for different audiences (Council of Europe 2020). This is highly relevant in India, where professionals regularly move between English documents and patients, clients or colleagues who speak other languages. NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 both value multilingualism and home languages as resources rather than obstacles (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). A nurse who can read an English discharge summary and explain it clearly in Kannada is showing exactly the competence the course should develop.
As with Unit 60, the aim of a checkpoint is one coherent, teachable plan, not a perfect one.

items: Needs analysis report. A genre priority map based on stakeholder interviews and learner data.
Course map. A twelve-week plan showing writing, listening, rich-text, mediation, assessment, research and materials strands.
Assessment plan. Task-specific rubrics and a written statement of realistic expectations.
Pilot record. One original material in two versions, with the pilot notes that explain the changes.
Which learners you teach have the clearest target situation? How well does your course reflect it?
Who could you interview to understand that situation better?
Where could mediation between languages become part of your course?
How clearly do you separate course aims from exam preparation?
What question about your course would you most like evidence on?

perm: The nursing course, care plans, discharge summaries, lecture extract, handover and all dialogues are written for this book; any resemblance to real patients is coincidental. Real workplace documents used in course design must be anonymized and used with the institution’s permission, and lecture recordings need the lecturers’ consent. Rich texts must be in the public domain or used with permission. Screenshots of Google tools, Audacity or Project Gutenberg require permission or replacement with original illustrations.
next: Coming next. Unit 71 opens Tier III's final stretch, turning to multilingualism and translanguaging in the classroom.

terms.def: In English for nursing, a written document recording a patient’s needs and planned nursing actions, used as an authentic target genre in designing a specific-purpose course.
A visual plan showing how a course is organized over time, with its strands, units and assessment points; it can be drawn on chart paper or kept as a colour-coded spreadsheet.

A written medical document given when a patient leaves hospital, setting out diagnosis, treatment and instructions. In a nursing English course it is a target genre, for example read in English and explained to the patient in Kannada.
A ranked list of the genres learners need in their target situation, based on needs analysis, such as a nursing course listing care plans, handovers and lectures in order of importance.
In nursing, the spoken and written transfer of patient information between shifts. In an English for Specific Purposes course for nurses, it is a high-priority spoken target genre.

1. In the CEFR, making meaning accessible to others, within or across languages, by relaying texts, explaining concepts or facilitating communication (Council of Europe 2020). 2. In sociocultural theory, the way tools, especially language, shape thinking and learning.
In ESP course design, the analysis of learners’ current language abilities, resources and learning situation at the start of a course.

Anyone with an interest in a course or its outcomes, such as learners, parents, teachers, employers, subject specialists or administrators. In course design, stakeholders are consulted during needs analysis.
An expert in the learners’ professional or academic field, such as a nurse, engineer or lawyer, with whom an ESP teacher collaborates on needs analysis, materials and assessment.

The part of needs analysis that identifies what learners will need to do in English in their target situation, including tasks, texts and skills (Hutchinson and Waters 1987). It is paired with present-situation analysis.
